search_summary: Searched the web for open problems on the fermion sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo and related many-body methods. Bohrium LKM was not searched: the `gaia` CLI is not installed in this environment (`gaia: command not found`, no binary in the project venv), so LKM routes were unavailable and only web-accessible primary sources were used. Queries covered: sign problem NP-hardness (Troyer-Wiese), complexity of curing non-stoquastic Hamiltonians, easing the sign problem via basis changes, sign problem at quantum critical points (DQMC), PIMC sign problem for degenerate fermions/warm dense matter, and the finite-density lattice QCD sign problem and QCD critical point. Inspected sources: arXiv abstract pages for cond-mat/0408370 (Troyer & Wiese, abstract), 2108.08974 (Mondaini, Tarat & Scalettar, abstract), 1906.02309 (Hangleiter et al., abstract), and 2007.05436 (Alexandru et al. RMP, abstract, used as corroboration); full HTML (ar5iv) of 1802.03408 (Marvian, Lidar & Hen, including its explicit Conclusions and open questions section), 2104.10032 (Dornheim et al., GCE PIMC), and 2108.12423 (Nagata review on finite-density lattice QCD, including its Open problems section). Coverage: complexity-theoretic status, practical severity/scaling in PIMC and DQMC, and the QCD finite-density sign problem; all five returned leads rest on abstract-level-or-stronger inspected material, three on full text. Outcome: five context-grounded leads spanning computational complexity of curing/easing the sign problem, the exponential PIMC wall for degenerate fermions, the doped Hubbard model's low average sign, and the QCD critical point blocked by the sign problem. Limits: no LKM claim/question retrieval was possible; later-literature current-status audits remain for the downstream pipeline.

problem_leads.proposed_question: What is the computational complexity of deciding whether a k-local non-stoquastic Hamiltonian can be cured (transformed into a stoquastic, sign-problem-free form) by a constant-depth quantum circuit that also allows two-qubit rotations, whether discrete or continuous — and can the NP-completeness of finding curing transformations, proven for 3-local and 6-local Hamiltonians under single-qubit Clifford or orthogonal rotations, be extended to 2-local Hamiltonians?

source.title: On the Computational Complexity of Curing the Sign Problem

problem_leads.exact_excerpt: It is important to clarify the computational complexity of finding the curing transformation in the case of constant-depth circuits that also allow two-body rotations, whether discrete or continuous.
problem_leads.surrounding_context: Marvian, Lidar and Hen prove that deciding whether a local Hamiltonian can be cured (made stoquastic, hence sign-problem-free for quantum Monte Carlo) is NP-complete when the allowed transformations are tensor products of single-qubit Clifford gates (3-local Hamiltonians, Theorem 1) or general single-qubit orthogonal matrices (6-local Hamiltonians, Theorem 2). In their 'Conclusions and open questions' section they state: 'It is important to clarify the computational complexity of finding the curing transformation in the case of constant-depth circuits that also allow two-body rotations, whether discrete or continuous. Also, since our NP-completeness proof involved 333 and 666-local Hamiltonians, it is interesting to try to reduce it to 222-local building blocks.' They further ask whether quantum algorithms can cure the sign problem more efficiently than classical ones, and conclude: 'We leave these as open questions to be addressed in future studies.' The 333/666/222 digit forms are ar5iv renderings of 3, 6, and 2 in the original text.
problem_leads.source_intent: The authors aim to re-found stoquasticity in complexity-theoretic terms ('computational stoquasticity'): after proving NP-completeness of curing under restricted single-qubit transformation classes, they explicitly flag richer transformation classes (constant-depth circuits with two-body rotations), lower locality (2-local), approximate curing (small positive off-diagonal elements), and quantum curing algorithms as unresolved extensions of their hardness results.
problem_leads.derivation_rationale: The proposed question restates the authors' own explicitly listed open questions without strengthening them: the hardness results are proven only for single-qubit transformation groups and 3-/6-local constructions, so the complexity of curing under constant-depth circuits with two-body rotations and for 2-local Hamiltonians is genuinely undecided by the paper. The question keeps the paper's decision-problem framing (does a curing transformation exist and how hard is it to find), which yields an unambiguous acceptance standard: a complexity classification (membership/hardness proof, algorithm, or counterexample) for the stated transformation class and locality.

evidence.supports: Direct: full HTML text inspected, including Theorems 1-2 (NP-completeness of curing under single-qubit Clifford and orthogonal transformations) and the explicit open-questions list quoted in the excerpt.

problem_leads.proposed_question: Can fermionic path integral Monte Carlo (or any related equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method) be made to compute thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems with computing cost that does not grow exponentially with particle number N and inverse temperature beta, given that the fermion sign problem causes an exponential increase of computing time and is NP-hard in the general case?

source.title: Fermion Sign Problem in Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulations: Grand-canonical ensemble

problem_leads.exact_excerpt: The antisymmetry of the fermionic density matrix under the exchange of particles leads to the notorious fermion sign problem (FSP) [25, 26], which is one of the most fundamental and challenging obstacles in theoretical physics and quantum chemistry.
problem_leads.surrounding_context: Dornheim analyzes the fermion sign problem in fermionic PIMC simulations of electrons in a 2D harmonic trap, in the grand-canonical ensemble. In the introduction he writes: 'The antisymmetry of the fermionic density matrix under the exchange of particles leads to the notorious fermion sign problem (FSP) [25, 26], which is one of the most fundamental and challenging obstacles in theoretical physics and quantum chemistry.' He then recalls the standard result S = exp(-beta N Delta f) for the average sign and states that this produces 'an exponential wall in fermionic PIMC simulations with respect to N and beta, which can only be compensated by increasing the amount of compute time as ~1/sqrt(N_MC), which inevitably becomes infeasible,' noting the problem 'has been revealed as NP-hard for some cases by Troyer and Wiese'. His new results show the sign problem is even more severe in the grand-canonical ensemble (super-exponential decay of the average sign with chemical potential and decreasing coupling) and that the bosonic reference simulation wastes effort in particle-number sectors irrelevant to fermions.
problem_leads.source_intent: The author's intent is a practical, quantitative characterization of how the fermion sign problem manifests in PIMC (dependence on temperature, chemical potential, coupling, and ensemble choice), documenting the exponential-to-super-exponential scaling of compute cost and the resulting infeasibility barrier for large, strongly degenerate fermionic systems — thereby identifying the barrier itself as the obstacle to be overcome.
problem_leads.derivation_rationale: The paper does not claim a generic solution is impossible — it cites Troyer-Wiese only for NP-hardness 'for some cases' — but demonstrates concretely that current fermionic PIMC methodology hits an exponential wall. The possible research question follows faithfully: whether this wall can be circumvented, i.e., whether there exists a method that computes thermal properties of degenerate fermions with sub-exponential cost. This preserves the source's full generality (no restriction to a specific model or temperature window is added). Acceptance is unambiguous: either a proof that no such polynomial-cost method exists (beyond the known special-case NP-hardness), or a construction demonstrated on degenerate fermionic systems with verified cost scaling.

authoritative_formulation.citation: M. Troyer and U.-J. Wiese, Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations, Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201 (2005), arXiv:cond-mat/0408370
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, while being efficient for bosons, suffer from the "negative sign problem'' when applied to fermions - causing an exponential increase of the computing time with the number of particles. A polynomial time solution to the sign problem is highly desired since it would provide an unbiased and numerically exact method to simulate correlated quantum systems. Here we show, that such a solution is almost certainly unattainable by proving that the sign problem is NP-hard, implying that a generic solution of the sign problem would also solve all problems in the complexity class NP (nondeterministic polynomial) in polynomial time.

evidence.supports: Direct: full HTML text inspected; documents the exponential wall of fermionic PIMC (S = exp(-beta N Delta f)), its NP-hardness citation, and the newly shown super-exponential severity in the grand-canonical ensemble.

Direct: abstract of Troyer & Wiese (PRL 94, 170201) inspected; states the exponential increase of computing time for fermions and the NP-hardness result, which bounds the meaning of a 'generic solution' for this lead.

problem_leads.proposed_question: What is the microscopic origin of the low average sign of the Hubbard model on the square lattice away from half-filling in determinant quantum Monte Carlo, and is its onset quantitatively linked to the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity?

source.title: Quantum Critical Points and the Sign Problem

problem_leads.exact_excerpt: We then propose a reinterpretation of the low average sign for the Hubbard model on the square lattice when away from half-filling, an important open problem in condensed matter physics, in terms of the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity.
problem_leads.surrounding_context: Mondaini, Tarat and Scalettar show that the sign problem in determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) is quantitatively linked to quantum critical behavior, via simulations of the spinful and spinless Hubbard models on the honeycomb lattice and the ionic Hubbard model. The abstract states: 'We then propose a reinterpretation of the low average sign for the Hubbard model on the square lattice when away from half-filling, an important open problem in condensed matter physics, in terms of the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity.' Their study 'charts a path for exploiting the average sign in QMC simulations to understand quantum critical behavior, rather than solely as an obstacle'.
problem_leads.source_intent: The authors' intent is to demonstrate that the severity (average sign) of the sign problem is tied to quantum criticality in several models, and to propose — as a reinterpretation of a problem they explicitly call an important open one — that the anomalously low average sign of the doped square-lattice Hubbard model reflects the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity, rather than being a purely numerical artifact.
problem_leads.derivation_rationale: The source itself labels the low average sign of the doped square-lattice Hubbard model 'an important open problem' and offers a proposed reinterpretation that is, by construction, not yet established. The derived question asks whether that reinterpretation is correct and quantitatively predictive. This is faithful: it neither upgrades the proposal to a conclusion nor narrows the model; it asks for the origin of the low average sign and a test of the proposed link to pseudogap/exotic-superconductivity onset. Acceptance is concrete: controlled DQMC (or complementary method) evidence establishing or refuting a quantitative correspondence between sign onset and pseudogap/superconducting onset, or a rigorous analysis of the sign structure of the doped Hubbard model.

evidence.supports: Direct: abstract inspected (Science 375, 418 (2022)); explicitly names the low average sign of the Hubbard model away from half-filling as an important open problem and states the proposed reinterpretation.

problem_leads.proposed_question: Does a QCD critical point exist in the temperature-baryon-chemical-potential phase diagram, and if it does, what are its critical temperature and density — a first-principles determination currently blocked by the sign problem of lattice QCD at nonzero quark chemical potential?

source.title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems

problem_leads.exact_excerpt: The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.
problem_leads.surrounding_context: Nagata's review (Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991 (2022)) surveys finite-density lattice QCD. In Section 1.1.1, discussing the QCD critical point as an open problem in baryonic matter: 'However, the QCD critical point has not been discovered so far. Although there are many phenomenological studies regarding the QCD critical point, the location of the critical point on the phase diagram is not known. Even the very existence is not established. The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.' The review explains the obstacle: 'When the quark chemical potential is nonzero, the Euclidean action becomes complex, and the importance sampling is not applicable. The problem that the importance sampling does not apply to the theories with complex action or non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is called the 'sign problem'' and notes that 'the complex Langevin method does not work there, and the Lefschetz thimble encounters a difficulty associated with the summation of multiple thimbles' precisely in the low-temperature high-density region where the critical point would lie.
problem_leads.source_intent: The author's intent is to give a critical status review of the sign problem in finite-density lattice QCD: to identify the existence and location of the QCD critical point as a major open problem of baryonic matter, and to document why every current method (reweighting, Taylor expansion, analytic continuation, canonical method, complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimble) fails or loses reliability exactly in the high-density region relevant to that determination.
problem_leads.derivation_rationale: The lead directly restates the author's explicitly stated open problem with its stated scope (existence/non-existence of the QCD critical point and, if existent, its critical temperature and density, from first principles). No parameter window or method restriction is added; the connection to the sign problem is the review's own documented reason the problem remains open. Acceptance is unambiguous: a controlled first-principles QCD calculation that either establishes the critical point with quantified (T, mu) values and systematics, or excludes its existence in the relevant region — or a rigorous no-go result.

authoritative_formulation.citation: K. Nagata, Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems, Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991 (2022), arXiv:2108.12423, Sec. 1.1.1
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: However, the QCD critical point has not been discovered so far. Although there are many phenomenological studies regarding the QCD critical point, the location of the critical point on the phase diagram is not known. Even the very existence is not established. The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.

evidence.supports: Direct: full HTML text of the review inspected, including Section 1.1.1 (open problems), Section 1.2 (history and failure of importance sampling at finite density), and statements on complex Langevin and Lefschetz thimble limitations in the high-density region.

problem_leads.proposed_question: For which physically motivated families of quantum many-body Hamiltonians does there exist a polynomial-time classical algorithm that finds efficiently computable basis changes easing the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem (in terms of measurable non-stoquasticity), given that easing is NP-complete in general for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices?

source.title: Easing the Monte Carlo sign problem

problem_leads.exact_excerpt: we prove that easing the sign problem in terms of those measures is in general an NP-complete task for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices by a polynomial reduction to the MAXCUT-problem. Intriguingly, easing remains hard even in cases in which we can efficiently assert that no exact solution exists.
problem_leads.surrounding_context: Hangleiter, Roth, Nagaj and Eisert (Science Advances 6, eabb8341 (2020)) develop 'a systematic, generally applicable, and practically feasible methodology for easing the sign problem by efficiently computable basis changes' and introduce measures of non-stoquasticity that serve as 'a practically relevant and efficiently computable figure of merit for the severity of the sign problem'. They demonstrate practical easing for frustrated Heisenberg ladders using geometric optimization over the orthogonal group. The abstract then states: 'we prove that easing the sign problem in terms of those measures is in general an NP-complete task for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices by a polynomial reduction to the MAXCUT-problem. Intriguingly, easing remains hard even in cases in which we can efficiently assert that no exact solution exists.' The hardness result is qualified as holding 'in general', leaving the complexity of easing for specific physically relevant Hamiltonian families unaddressed.
problem_leads.source_intent: The authors' intent is twofold: to provide a practical, measure-driven methodology that eases the sign problem in concrete models, and to delineate its fundamental limits by proving worst-case NP-completeness of the easing task — thereby framing the boundary between practically tractable easing and generic intractability.
problem_leads.derivation_rationale: The NP-completeness result is explicitly generic ('in general ... for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices'), so it does not settle the complexity or feasibility of easing for structured, physically motivated Hamiltonian families — the regime where the paper's own methodology succeeds for Heisenberg ladders. The derived question asks precisely for that classification, staying within the paper's measure-based definition of easing. Acceptance is concrete: either polynomial-time easing algorithms with demonstrated sign improvement for a specified physically motivated family, or family-specific hardness/impossibility results.

evidence.supports: Direct: abstract inspected; documents both the practical easing methodology for frustrated Heisenberg ladders and the NP-completeness of easing in general, quoted verbatim in the excerpt.
